title: MIS reforms must avoid added burdens
full_text:
SMSF trustees are investors in managed investment schemes (MIS) and as consumers should not be expected to hold or provide information about these vehicles that should be held by other entities, the SMSF Association has told the government.
The professional body made the statement in a submission to Treasury’s consultation on proposals to improve the regulatory visibility of the MIS sector through enhanced data collection, which is part of a set of consumer protection measures for super fund members announced by Financial Services Minister Daniel Mulino last month.
“In designing the framework, our key concern is the regulatory burden should sit with the entities that generate, hold and can reliably report the relevant data,” the submission stated.
“SMSFs should not be required to duplicate information responsible entities, platforms, Australian financial services licensees or other regulated intermediaries can provide.”
In making explicit recommendations, the association called for a clear separation of SMSFs from other entities when it came to the use of MIS and thus how data was collected.
“Distinguish the source or beneficial investor type from the distribution pathway. For example, an investment may ultimately be funded by an SMSF but reach the MIS through a platform or adviser. Those are different data points and should not be conflated,” the submission stated.
“Do not impose new reporting obligations on SMSF trustees merely because SMSFs are an identifiable source of MIS investment. Where a responsible entity, platform or regulated intermediary provides the information, collect it there.”
The association noted while it supported further reforms within the MIS sector, the collection of data had to be an initial starting point leading to further action.
“The value of these reforms lies in whether better information enables regulators to identify emerging risks and intervene before losses become widespread. Data collection should therefore be treated as regulatory infrastructure for prevention, not as an end in itself,” it added.
“The recent reform program has highlighted that consumer harm can arise through an interconnected chain involving lead generation, financial advice, superannuation switching, platforms and the underlying MIS.
“Better data can help regulators identify emerging risks across that chain. However, any additional data collection should be designed around demonstrated supervisory use cases and must lead to timely action where material risks are identified.
“For SMSF trustees, the objective should be stronger protection from misconduct and product failure without treating the SMSF structure itself as the source of risk or imposing unnecessary new obligations on trustees who are investors in the system.”
author: Jason Spits
heading: Superannuation and Investments
